knowledge_delta.summary: Twelve-Factor adds a process-lifetime boundary rather than another workflow runtime: compute processes are disposable, durable correctness state belongs in backing services, and local memory/files are acceptable only when their loss is safe.

items.label: Stateless process
items.source_basis: The source states that twelve-factor processes are stateless/share-nothing and cannot assume future requests or jobs return to the same process.
items.prior_basis: The graph had implementation-specific Worker and Workflow concepts but no generic disposable-process runtime boundary.
items.interpretation: Stateless process becomes a reusable architecture concept about process lifetime, independent of any one orchestration technology.

items.label: Backing-service state
items.source_basis: Any data that must persist is stored in a stateful backing service rather than process memory or local filesystem.
items.prior_basis: No prior concept explicitly represented the application-level rule that durable correctness state must survive outside disposable compute processes.
items.interpretation: The application can remain stateful while compute stays replaceable because persistence has an explicit external owner.

items.label: Ephemeral process state
items.source_basis: Memory and local filesystem may be used as brief single-transaction cache but must not be required by future requests/jobs.
items.prior_basis: The existing graph did not distinguish safe temporary process-local working data from durable application state.
items.interpretation: This avoids the overcorrection that stateless architecture forbids all local state; the real test is whether losing it breaks correctness.

claims.text: Twelve-factor application processes are stateless and share-nothing, so correctness must not depend on hidden state retained inside one process instance across requests or jobs.

evidence.locator: VI. Processes → stateless and share-nothing processes

claims.text: Data that must persist beyond the current process work unit belongs in a stateful backing service rather than only in process memory or local filesystem.

evidence.locator: VI. Processes → persistent data in a stateful backing service

claims.text: Process memory or filesystem may be used as brief temporary cache only when future requests or jobs do not depend on that local state surviving restart, relocation or process replacement.

evidence.locator: VI. Processes → memory/filesystem as brief single-transaction cache

claims.text: The stateless-process principle is compatible with durable workflows when orchestration state lives outside disposable workers, but the Twelve-Factor source itself does not define a durable workflow execution mechanism.

evidence.locator: VI. Processes → stateless/share-nothing and persistent backing-service state
Durable Workflow Execution state outside replaceable Worker Processes

claims.note: The source establishes disposable process-local state; compatibility with Temporal-style external durable workflow state is project synthesis and should not be read as a source claim.

prerequisite_map.summary: The model needs only three pieces: a disposable stateless process, a backing service that owns persistent state, and an explicit category of ephemeral local working data whose loss is safe.

items.label: Stateless process
items.reason: The factor is fundamentally about making process instances disposable across requests, jobs, restarts and scaling.

items.label: Backing-service state
items.reason: Without external persistent state, 'stateless process' is easily misread as an application with no durable state at all.

items.label: Ephemeral process state
items.reason: The source explicitly allows process-local cache when losing it is safe, which defines the practical boundary rather than a blanket ban on local state.

learning_prompt.retention_prompt: Without looking back, reconstruct the Twelve-Factor process boundary: explain why future requests/jobs cannot rely on one process instance, where persistent application state belongs, what process-local state is still allowed, and why this does not mean the whole application is stateless.

transfer_prompt.prompt: A service is scaled to five interchangeable instances and a multi-step job may resume after a restart. Decide which data can remain local, which state must move to an external durable service, and what property makes an instance genuinely disposable.

source_decision.rationale: The original Processes page is very short and the explainer preserves its complete conceptual argument: stateless/share-nothing processes, persistent backing-service state, disposable local cache, restart boundaries and the sticky-session warning. Reopening the source adds little unless the canonical wording itself is needed.

novelty.reason: The source adds a generic runtime-process disposability model rather than another implementation-specific workflow or worker concept.

source_quality.reason: The primary source is the canonical Twelve-Factor Processes page authored by Adam Wiggins and fully inspected.

relevance.reason: The process/state boundary remains directly useful for horizontally scaled services, background workers and containerized deployments.

practical_leverage.reason: The model gives a concrete review test: if losing one process breaks future correctness, durable state has been placed at the wrong lifetime boundary.

compression_loss.reason: The source itself is compact and contains no large implementation sections that must be preserved for the requested mental model.
